thread.title: Stocks Edge Lower After Inflation News

author: Barron's
title: Stocks Edge Lower After Inflation News
text:
Getty Images Inflation Conversation. Stocks were modestly lower but little changed on Wednesday following the release of the August Producer Price Index, while on the equity side all eyes remain on Apple 's ( AAPL ) product launch. In today's Morning Movers, we…
•Review the PPI reading;
•Consider what it means for the Fed;
•And look in on what's lifting Chevron ( CVX ).
Looking for Direction
Stocks were slipping slightly in early trading Wednesday, after the PPI showed wholesale inflation fell for the first time in a year and a half.
Dow Jones Industrial Average futures and S&P 500 futures, and Nasdaq Composite futures were just a little shy of flat, with the latter nosing occasionally into small gains.
The PPI declined by 0.1% last month, according to Labor Department data, compared to the 0.2% increase economists were expecting, the first drop since February 2017. And while the decline stemmed from the generally volatile services category (which includes retail and transportation) the increase in wholesale inflation over the past year was also down, to 2.8% from 3.4%. That's a relief from the seven-year high we notched two months ago. Yet the core PPI, which strips out lumpier categories like energy, rose 0.1% last month, while the one-year rate climbed to 2.9%, on par with its 2018 high.
The PPI reading will be the "clincher," for the Federal Reserve's rate-increase regime, as inflation has taken center stage over employment, writes Tigress Financial's Jean Ergas. Wage growth has already hinted that the "labor reservoir is starting to slowly be drained…cementing" Fed policy, he notes, and the central bank isn't yet concerned enough about emerging markets' pain to change course. So Wednesday's data, while not matching expectations exactly, is likely just more fuel for that fire (as stocks' muted reaction confirms).
Nor does the Fed seem particularly bothered by the yield curve, for all the fuss elsewhere about it, with New York Fed President John Williams saying that the central bank would move interest rates up to the point the yield curve is flat or inverted, if its mandate calls for it.
Yet MKM Partner's Michael Darda writes that the Fed should tread with caution. While Williams may think it's different this time around, citing global quantitative easing that has distorted yields, it's never really different, he says. "The Fed has an unenviable history of ignoring inversions with theories that sound reasonable at the time, but with recessions following in one or two years anyway (see 1989, 2000, and 2006 for recent examples.)"
Still, it's hard to blame the Fed for feeling confident, given all the positive recent data, which stands in stark contrast to other economies around the globe. The good mood among investors fits with the idea that the U.S. is poised for good times regardless of what happens elsewhere, an idea reinforced by Tuesday's record reading on small business optimism. While the rest of the world struggles, key data points for August, from consumer confidence to payrolls, have underscored the strength of the domestic economy, writes NatWest Markets' Michelle Girard.
"In this way, rather than a one-off "sugar high," we believe the stage is set for sustained growth in the U.S.," she writes.
Indeed, just Wednesday, The Wall Street Journal highlighted the strength in transport stocks, a trend Barron's noted last month, as evidence that stocks can keep pushing toward new highs. Let's keep on trucking.
